newsitem.title: GREECE: ATHLETICS-GREEKS COULD BE IN TROUBLE OVER BANNERS.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-GREEKS COULD BE IN TROUBLE OVER BANNERS.

text.p: Athletics officials may be forced to take action against supporters of Athen's bid for the 2004 Olympics after scores of people held up a huge banner in the stadium during the opening two days of the world championships.
The International Amateur Athletic Federation (IAAF) does not allow advertising from any of the five cities bidding for the Games in the stadium at the championships.
But spectators held up a banner with the official logo of the Athens bid which was clearly visible to the television cameras on Saturday and Sunday.
Athens 2004 bid Officials said the incident was likely to be repeated each day of the championships.

Although the people who held the banner above their heads across a block of seats opposite the main stand were not directly linked to the Athens bid, IAAF general secretary Istvan Gyulai described it as "excessive."

"If it happens again in the future we will have to discuss it," Gyulai said before the supporters repeated the incident in the middle of Sunday evening's session when the 100 metres sprint finals were due to take place.
"There is no rule on this. But our policy is not to accept advertising from a bidding committee. But there has been no official protest (to Athens)."

Officials from the Athens bid committee, which is competing with Rome, Buenos Aires, Cape Town and Stockholm for the Games, said they believed the supporters were volunteers from a local newspaper which is backing the bid.

"It has nothing to do with the Athens bidding committee. They bought the tickets and put up the banner," one Athens 2004 official said. "I believe they have the right to do that. We hear that they plan to repeat it every day."

Athens is staging the most prestigious athletics event outside of the Olympic Games at a key moment in the bidding process. The International Olympic Committee (IOC) will decide next month who will host the 2004 Summer Games.
The Greek capital is regarded as being a serious threat to favourites Rome and events at the world championships could influence the outcome of the vote.
The attendances in the first two days of the event would have been disappointing for both the IAAF and the organisers.
Barely more than 3,000 people watched Michael Johnson start his 400 metres campaign on Sunday morning.
The stadium was only half full shortly before the men's and women's 100 metres finals, two of the most attractive races of the competition.

"This has surprised us since we were told that 75 per cent of the tickets had been sold," Gyulai said after Sunday's morning session. "I was flabbergasted (by the low numbers). But we will have to see if it is an exceptional case."
